content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper presents to use contrastive learning methods in the latent space of the variational autoencoder model for image generation, and in a continual learning setting. The training is divided into two procedures. In the learning phase, an autoencoder model is trained under reconstruction loss, and in the partitioning phase, the decoder is adjusted under reconstruction loss + triplet loss. The triplet loss is formulated based on pseudo labels from model prediction. The performance of the model is evaluated on the quality of the generated image, using the FID score and overlap of the distributions between generated data and the real data. Experimental evaluation includes MNIST, FashionMNIST, and CelebA datasets.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
It is an interesting idea to use contrastive learning in continual learning, with a particular focus on image generation or reconstruction. Probably, the title can be refined, and add “image generation” to indicate the score of work more accurately. The paper presents a well-written literature review on continual learning, covering regularization, rehearsal/replay, memory-based, and other contrastive learning-based methods. The downside of this paper include 

(1) the formal setup of continual learning is missing. It seems the model is under the class-incremental setup where a new task means images from new categories, but this needs to be made clear. For example, how many MINIST or FashionMNIST classes are provided for each task? 

(2) the evaluation in the context of continual learning is missing. For example, the aspect of catastrophic forgetting and model performance if it was trained and evaluated under a sequence of tasks. Especially, whether the encoder is transferrable between tasks or every round it needs to be retrained from the scratch.  It is also helpful to add more baseline comparisons to other deep generative models in similar settings, such as Cong, Yulai, et al. "Gan memory with no forgetting." *Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems* 33 (2020): 16481-16494.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
There are many important technical details missing or unclear.
(1) How the class id is predicted? What kind of model is used? How many classes are allowed, and could it handle the increasing number of classes? 

(2) How the intersection of distributions is computed in computing the precision and recall? Does it require generating samples from the model and training an external classifier on real or generated?  Although Figure 4 and a citation to Kynkaanniemi et al 2019 are given, it is still unclear.  It would be helpful to describe how this is done and make this paper self-contained. 

(3) What exactly is the generative process of images from the trained auto-encoder?
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, the paper suffers from several clarity issues and important baselines are missing. It also lacks evaluations in the continual learning setting. It would also be more helpful to eventually evaluate the proposed approach on continual learning benchmark datasets such as CORe50 NICv2.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.summary_of_the_paper: A metric-learning model w.r.t. triplet loss is formulated for continual learning. This paper mainly focuses on building useful latent space. Experiments on different datasets show its effectiveness.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
A discriminative latent space is formulated based on triplet loss for continual learning. The overall learning framework is simple yet effective from the idea and experiments. 

Weakness:
This paper follows the previous deep metric learning model for continual learning in Cha et al. 2021. The previous work built their model by using contrastive learning for classification. In contrast, this work is formalized on VAE with triplet latent space construction. The other learning tricks are similar to the previous one. 

Bigger datasets are necessary, and these presented datasets are too simple for current classification tasks.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper studies continual learning, where a model cannot train on all training data repeatedly. The authors propose to apply triplet loss to do latent space portioning towards solving the forgetting problem. The proposed method consists of two phases, wherein the first phase learns the current task and the second phase refines the knowledge of current and previous tasks via applying triplet loss.

The authors claim achieving better performance than previous methods on MNIST and FashionMNIST, and performed ablation studies on CelebA.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The paper is interesting. The triplet loss is a reasonable choice to tackle the latent space overlapping issue. The authors also claim they do not use generative replay and do not store the samples and representations of samples of previous tasks, which is memory efficient. 
 
However, I do have below concerns which are the potential weaknesses of the paper.

1.  First of all, the key contributions/implementations are described in the first half of page 6, and I found some information is missing. For example, the authors mentioned “Divide the decoder into front layers and back layers”, and “Front layers set to be one-tenth of LR of back layers, which is the warm-up stage of the portioning phase”. Given a multi-layer decoder, how do you decide which layer should be the latent layer? How many epochs do you need for the warm-up stage, or what’s the criteria to stop the warm-up stage? How do you measure the distance of two latent variables in equation 3?

2. I found the sentences ‘As for getting the latent spaces, we just use the model itself to generate some data, which includes latent spaces, predicted class id, etc.’ very vaguely described. As you said you don’t store any real samples or latent variables of previous tasks, do you only always transform samples from current tasks into latent representations? How do you define ‘predicted class id’? What if the current new task introduces a new class id that you are not aware of in previous tasks? What concerns me most is that, in continual learning, the sequential tasks/data may have incremental classes, or partially same classes, or even totally different classes. Handling those complicated scenarios are not reflected in either the experiments, or not illustrated in the main figure (figure 3).

3. I would also recommend the authors to compare and contrast with the Multiband VAE paper in their introduction or related work sections.
 
I also have some questions/concerns on the evaluation part. 

1. First of all, congratulations for achieving good performance on MNIST and FashionMNIST. 

2. Why do you only compare with other methods on MNIST and FashionMNIST, but not CelebA? 

3. And what’s your motivation to ignore Mmniglot?

4. In order to examine the catastrophic forgetting, and really claim that your method outperforms Multiband VAE, I would encourage the authors to follow their experimental setup (e.g., how to split examples from the same classes into different tasks).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
-- The authors mentioned that “Triplet loss is the most widely used loss function in deep metric learning”. Maybe saying “one of”?

-- Page 2, “consider a model as a function and computer the importance of parameters”

-- I found z, o, c, and lambda are interchangeably used in different contexts to denote (presumably different stages) of latent variables, which is a little bit confusing.
content.summary_of_the_review: I found the paper overall interesting; However, due to the aforementioned concerns, I’m not sure the paper is ready for publishing at ICLR. I’m happy to discuss and revise my evolutions.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
Summary
The authors consider the problem of continual learning. They focus on alleviating the issue of catastrophic forgetting.
Jointly training the model on the data of all tasks comes with various issues of limitations of memory, privacy issues, etc. Hence continual learning is adopted where the model is trained incrementally on the tasks one by one.
Under continual setup, the model tends to forget previously learned knowledge about previous tasks. This phenomenon is called catastrophic forgetting.
The authors propose to partition the latent space to avoid overlapping between classes using triplet loss.
The proposed method consists of two phases, viz, learning and partitioning.
In the learning phase, the model is purely trained on the current task. The loss function used is the one proposed by Kingma and Welling (2013). (VAE loss: Cross entropy and mean squared error).
In the partitioning phase, the latent space is partitioned to avoid the overlap between different classes hence in turn alleviating the catastrophic forgetting problem. In this phase, the encoder is frozen. The decoder is divided into two parts: layers between the encoder and the latent layer and layers between the latent layer and the output layer. In the warm phase, the first part of the decoder is trained with 1/10 of the learning rate as that of the second part. After the warm-up stage, the whole decoder will be trained with the same learning rate. The loss function used is triplet loss proposed by Shroff et al.
The triplet loss helps in adjusting the distance between the latent variables depending on the corresponding class labels
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
The problem of continual learning considered and the issues of catastrophic forgetting highlighted are very relevant.
The flow of the prior work is presented well with various issues in the existing methods properly discussed.
          
The authors demonstrate the validity of their work, i.e., you can avoid performance drop through experimental results. The proposed method outperforms all the considered baseline methods.
The importance of triplet loss under continual learning is well explained in Fig. (1).
How the proposed method partitions the latent space is well illustrated in Fig. (3) and (5).



Weaknesses:

The method is decent but not very novel. They use triplet loss proposed by Shroff et al for latent space partitioning.
They should clarify that by “different classes” they mean “different tasks”
They don’t discuss how the proposed method is better than the one proposed by cha et al 2021 and don’t mention the drawbacks of this method in prior work.
The paragraph on deep metric learning applied to other problems in prior work) is not that relevant, otherwise, the prior work is written well.
In figure 2, (b) partitioning phase, it seems Oi and Oi′ are swapped.
Why training is done in two phases? These two could be clubbed together and trained with all loss functions in one phase. The authors don't discuss this.
The authors don't specify how they are generating data belonging to different tasks during the partitioning phase.
They don’t discuss the complexities (say # params) of various models considered.
The authors don’t specify why they are not comparing with the method of Cha et al. 2021. This involves deep metric learning/contrastive learning applied to continual learning setup.
            
In the caption of table 3, the phrase “other baseline methods” should be dropped.
There are a few typos and many of the sentences should be rewritten properly.
